drills.q: Name three GRASP patterns and what question each answers.
drills.a: Information Expert (who owns behavior given the data it needs), Creator (who instantiates X), Controller (what receives a system-boundary event and delegates), among others like Low/High Cohesion, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, Protected Variations.

drills.q: Two validation functions are byte-identical today. A teammate says 'DRY this up.' What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether they represent the same underlying knowledge/policy or are coincidentally identical because they solve unrelated problems the same way right now — merging coincidental duplication creates false coupling that surfaces as boolean flags and branches when they diverge.

drills.q: What's wrong with using KISS to justify removing a bounds check on a discount percentage input?
drills.a: KISS argues against unnecessary structural complexity, not against correctness guarantees. A missing bounds check is a latent bug (e.g. pct=1.5 makes total negative), not simplicity.

drills.q: Explain how YAGNI can be correct at the team level and still produce an org-level failure.
drills.a: Every team correctly skips building shared cross-cutting infrastructure (e.g. an event schema registry) because their own immediate need doesn't justify it. In aggregate, nobody builds it until multiple teams need it simultaneously during an incident, costing more than early investment would have — a coordination failure, not a flaw in YAGNI's per-team logic.

drills.q: Fix this Law of Demeter violation: order.customer.billing_address.country.tax_treaty_exempt
drills.a: Delegate one hop at a time: order.is_tax_treaty_exempt(), where Order asks Customer, which asks Address. Each object reaches only one level deep so a refactor of Address only touches Customer.

drills.q: When is strictly enforcing the Law of Demeter the wrong call?
drills.a: Inside a single cohesive aggregate that changes as a unit — forcing delegation methods for every internal traversal produces wrapper explosion with no real encapsulation benefit since the whole aggregate changes together anyway.

drills.q: A Penguin subclass of Bird overrides fly() to throw NotImplementedError. Diagnose and fix using composition.
drills.a: This models 'is-a' for taxonomy when callers depend on behavior (an LSP violation). Fix: extract flight as a FlightBehavior strategy injected into Bird; Penguin composes a CannotFly behavior instead of inheriting and overriding to fail.

drills.q: What is Pure Fabrication and how does it differ from the anemic-domain-model mistake?
drills.a: Pure Fabrication invents a non-domain class (e.g. PricingEngine) purely for cohesion/coupling reasons — appropriate for cross-cutting orchestration/infrastructure logic. It differs from the anemic-domain mistake, which extracts an entity's own invariant-protecting logic externally; that should stay on the entity.

drills.q: A teammate proposes a shared BaseEntity class with common CRUD methods inherited by every domain entity. Critique it.
drills.a: If it's truly shared mechanical data (id, created_at, equality) a shared base is fine. If 'CRUD methods' means persistence behavior, prefer composition (inject a repository per entity) since persistence constraints diverge per entity and a shared base will accumulate overridden methods that throw or no-op — the same LSP smell as Penguin/Bird.

drills.q: Rank DRY, KISS, YAGNI by how often each is invoked incorrectly in real code review, and explain why.
drills.a: DRY is misapplied most often because similarity is visible immediately while knowledge-vs-coincidence requires business context; KISS second, usually to skip a guard rather than an abstraction; YAGNI least often at the individual level since its failure mode is structural/org-level rather than a per-PR reflex.
